title: Interpretable Analytic Formulae for GWTC-4 Binary Black Hole Population Properties via Symbolic Regression
summary: Recent LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) analyses have revealed complex structure in the binary black hole (BBH) population, including distinct features in the primary mass spectrum and nontrivial spin-mass correlations. However, the phenomenological models used to capture these features often lack analytic transparency, making it difficult to isolate robust physical laws from modeling artifacts. To address this, symbolic regression is applied to the posterior inference products of the GWTC-4 catalog, discovering compact, closed-form analytic expressions for four key population relationships: (i) the merger-rate evolution with redshift; (ii) the mass-ratio dependence of the effective-spin distribution; (iii) the redshift evolution of the effective-spin distribution; and (iv) the conditional mass-ratio distributions associated with the 10 solar mass and 35 solar mass primary mass peaks. This framework successfully compresses both rigid and highly flexible models into differentiable phenomenological laws, dynamically recovering a consistent low-redshift merger-rate slope without assuming an a priori power-law form. The exact analytic derivatives provided by symbolic regression show that the mass ratio--effective spin and redshift--effective spin correlations are robustly driven by broadening of the posterior widths rather than shifts in the mean. Furthermore, qualitatively distinct functional forms for the mass-ratio distributions conditioned on the 10 solar mass and 35 solar mass primary mass peaks are identified. These closed-form expressions enable exact analytic gradient diagnostics and compact surrogate summaries, particularly for flexible numerical posteriors that are not otherwise available in low-dimensional analytic form. They also facilitate rapid downstream calculations for rate forecasting, formation channel comparison, and stochastic background estimation.

AI.tldr: Symbolic regression provides transparent analytic models for complex binary black hole population features from GWTC-4 data, improving interpretability and enabling precise analytic diagnostics and rapid downstream astrophysical applications.
AI.motivation: To discover compact, closed-form analytic expressions for complex population relationships in binary black hole data, addressing lack of analytic transparency in current phenomenological models
AI.method: Symbolic regression applied to posterior inference products of the GWTC-4 catalog
AI.result: Identification of analytic expressions for merger-rate evolution with redshift, mass-ratio dependence of effective-spin distribution, redshift evolution of effective-spin, and conditional mass-ratio distributions for specific primary mass peaks; providing exact analytic derivatives and revealing that certain correlations are due to broader posterior widths not mean shifts
AI.conclusion: Symbolic regression effectively compresses complex and flexible phenomenological models into closed-form analytic laws, enabling robust interpretation of BBH population structures and facilitating efficient further analyses in gravitational wave astrophysics.

title: Relativistic effects in k-essence
summary: Relativistic effects are sensitive to subtle changes in dark energy. These effects grow on very large scales and at high redshifts, which will be the reach of upcoming surveys. We investigate these effects in both the linear and the angular galaxy power spectra in a late-time universe dominated by cold dark matter and k-essence, focusing on three core models (dilaton, tachyon, and DBI scalar fields) and contrasting their predictions with those of the concordance model. By enforcing identical present-day cosmological parameters, we isolate the imprints of k-essence dynamics and perturbations on very large scales. We found that relativistic corrections dominate on very large scales and grow with redshift, but are largely insensitive to k-essence microphysics in Fourier space, leading to strong degeneracies among the models. However, in the angular power spectrum, where line-of-sight integrals are naturally included, relativistic effects are significantly amplified, yielding better sensitivity to clustering k-essence. In particular, the tachyon exhibits clear deviations across multipoles and redshifts, with distinct imprints in the Doppler and the combined (velocity and gravitational) potentials contributions. Furthermore, our results show that neglecting relativistic corrections can lead to systematic misestimation of deviations of k-essence from the cosmological constant. Our results show the relativistic angular galaxy power spectrum as a more consistent and robust probe of ultra-large-scale physics. These findings underscore the need for full relativistic modelling in next-generation surveys that are targeting horizon-scale modes, where the imprint of non-standard dark energy is most pronounced.

AI.tldr: Relativistic corrections significantly impact galaxy power spectra at large scales and high redshift, with angular spectra providing a sensitive probe for k-essence dark energy models. Ignoring these leads to biased results, emphasizing the necessity of relativistic modeling in upcoming surveys.
AI.motivation: To understand how subtle relativistic effects on large scales and high redshifts can reveal distinctive imprints of k-essence dark energy models, improving observational sensitivity beyond the concordance model and informing next-generation cosmological surveys targeting horizon-scale physics.
AI.method: The study analyzes relativistic effects on both linear and angular galaxy power spectra in a late-time cold dark matter universe with k-essence fields (dilaton, tachyon, DBI), enforcing identical present-day cosmological parameters to isolate k-essence effects. It contrasts predictions with the concordance model and evaluates Fourier versus angular spectra sensitivities across redshifts and multipoles.
AI.result: The paper examines relativistic effects on galaxy power spectra in a universe dominated by cold dark matter and k-essence, focusing on three scalar field models (dilaton, tachyon, DBI) compared to the concordance model. By fixing present-day cosmological parameters, it isolates k-essence signatures on large scales, finding that relativistic corrections dominate at very large scales and high redshift but show degeneracies in Fourier space. Angular power spectra, incorporating line-of-sight integrals, enhance sensitivity to clustering k-essence effects, particularly highlighting distinct tachyon deviations. Neglecting relativistic corrections risks systematic errors in assessing k-essence departures from the cosmological constant. The study advocates full relativistic modeling for future large-scale surveys probing horizon-scale modes.
AI.conclusion: Relativistic angular galaxy power spectra offer a robust and consistent method to detect ultra-large-scale signatures of k-essence dark energy. Full relativistic treatment is essential to avoid systematic biases and improve sensitivity in next-generation horizon-scale surveys.

title: Cosmological Gravitational Waves from Ultralight Vector Dark Matter
summary: We compute the abundance of cosmological gravitational waves produced during the evolution of an ultralight vector (spin-1) dark matter field. A homogeneous background vector field breaks spatial isotropy, requiring a Bianchi I geometry and inducing a mixing between the scalar, vector, and tensor perturbation sectors. We derive the perturbation equations in this background and show that, as a consequence of this mixing, scalar perturbations act as a source of tensor modes, generating a stochastic GW background. The production and cosmological evolution of these gravitational waves are implemented in a modified version of CLASS, from which we obtain the present-day spectrum.

AI.tldr: This paper studies gravitational waves generated by an ultralight vector dark matter field, focusing on how its anisotropic background produces a stochastic gravitational wave background.
AI.motivation: To understand how an ultralight vector dark matter field, which breaks spatial isotropy, affects gravitational wave production and to characterize the resulting cosmological gravitational wave background.
AI.method: The study derives perturbation equations in a Bianchi I geometry induced by the vector field's anisotropy, analyzing scalar, vector, and tensor mode mixing, and implements gravitational wave production and evolution numerically in modified CLASS.
AI.result: The derived perturbation equations demonstrate scalar modes sourcing tensor modes, leading to a stochastic gravitational wave background with a computable present-day spectrum.
AI.conclusion: The scalar perturbations sourced by the anisotropic ultralight vector dark matter field generate a stochastic gravitational wave background, with a present-day spectrum computed via a modified CLASS code.

title: Impact of the Infrared Cutoff on Structure Formation in Tsallis Holographic Dark Energy
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures. Comments, especially pointing out missing citations, are welcome
summary: We investigate the viability of Tsallis holographic dark energy (THDE) models, focusing on the role of the infrared (IR) cutoff in the growth of cosmic structures. Considering two commonly used choices of the cutoff, the particle horizon and the future event horizon, we analyze the evolution of linear matter perturbations and compute the growth factor, growth rate, and the observable $fσ_8(z)$. These predictions are compared with observational data from redshift-space distortion measurements. We find that the growth history is highly sensitive to the choice of IR cutoff. Models based on the future event horizon are consistent with observational data and can provide a fit comparable to, or slightly better than, the $Λ$CDM model for suitable values of the Tsallis parameter $δ$. In contrast, models constructed using the particle horizon generally fail to reproduce the observed growth of structure. These results demonstrate that the viability of THDE models depends crucially on the choice of IR cutoff and highlight the importance of structure formation as a stringent test of generalized holographic dark energy scenarios.

AI.tldr: The viability of Tsallis holographic dark energy models strongly depends on the chosen infrared cutoff; using the future event horizon yields models consistent with observations, while the particle horizon does not.
AI.motivation: To investigate the viability of THDE models in explaining cosmic structure growth and to assess how the choice of IR cutoff affects their compatibility with observational data, given the importance of understanding dark energy and structure formation in cosmology.
AI.method: We analyze the evolution of linear matter perturbations in Tsallis holographic dark energy (THDE) models by considering two infrared (IR) cutoff choices: the particle horizon and the future event horizon. We compute the growth factor, growth rate, and observable $fσ_8(z)$, and compare these theoretical predictions with observational data from redshift-space distortion measurements.
AI.result: Models with the future event horizon as the IR cutoff are consistent with observational data and can match or slightly improve upon the fit provided by the standard $Λ$CDM model for appropriate Tsallis parameter values. In contrast, models using the particle horizon fail to reproduce observed structure growth.
AI.conclusion: The choice of IR cutoff critically determines the compatibility of THDE models with observed cosmic structure formation, establishing the future event horizon-based models as viable alternatives to the $Λ$CDM paradigm and underscoring the role of growth history as a stringent test for generalized holographic dark energy scenarios.

title: Cosmological discrete self-similarity in primordial black hole formation
summary: We demonstrate that discrete self-similarity (DSS), originally discovered in the collapse of a massless scalar field in an asymptotically flat system, survives in primordial black hole (PBH) formation within an expanding cosmological background. Using fully relativistic numerical simulations of massless scalar-field collapse in an Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker universe, we resolve the critical regime down to $|p-p_c|\sim 10^{-8}$, where $p$ and $p_c$ respectively are a parameter of the family of initial data and its threshold value, and find clear log-periodic oscillations in the PBH mass scaling relation. The detailed structure of these oscillations differs from that previously reported in the asymptotically flat case, exhibiting a more pronounced asymmetry between peaks and troughs. Analyzing two distinct families of initial data (Gaussian and piecewise rational curvature profiles), we find critical exponents and DSS periods that differ slightly but are broadly consistent within uncertainties. The presence of DSS implies characteristic log-periodic modulations in the PBH mass spectrum, with potential consequences for PBH abundances and the spectrum of induced gravitational waves.

AI.tldr: This study shows that discrete self-similarity, known from scalar field collapse in flat spacetime, persists in primordial black hole formation in an expanding universe, producing log-periodic mass scaling patterns that affect PBH abundance and gravitational wave signals.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether discrete self-similarity (DSS), observed in scalar field collapse in asymptotically flat spacetimes, also occurs in primordial black hole formation in an expanding cosmological background.
AI.method: Performed fully relativistic numerical simulations of massless scalar-field collapse in a Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) universe, resolving the critical regime with parameter tuning down to |p - p_c| ~ 10^{-8}, and analyzed log-periodic oscillations in the PBH mass scaling relation.
AI.result: Confirmed that DSS survives in PBH formation within an expanding universe, observed clear log-periodic oscillations in the PBH mass scaling relation with detailed structure differing from asymptotically flat cases; found critical exponents and DSS periods broadly consistent across different initial data families.
AI.conclusion: Discrete self-similarity is a robust feature of primordial black hole formation in an expanding cosmological background, leading to characteristic log-periodic modulations in the PBH mass spectrum, which impacts predictions of PBH abundances and induced gravitational wave spectra.

title: Gravity Echoes from Supermassive Black Hole Binaries
summary: Pulsar timing arrays record gravitational waves from supermassive black hole binaries at two spacetime points: an Earth term, measured when the wave passes the Earth, and a pulsar term, measured when the wave passed each pulsar at an earlier epoch. We show that a future $μ$Hz-band detection of a nearby massive binary by a mission such as $μ$Ares would turn PTA pulsar terms into targeted probes of binary evolution. In analogy with supernova light echoes, each pulsar term acts as a gravity echo: a dated snapshot of the binary at an earlier stage of its inspiral. Together, the $μ$Hz Earth-term measurement and the nHz pulsar-term echoes provide a temporal baseline that neither detector could access alone. For a fiducial equal-mass binary with total mass $10^9\,M_\odot$ at 80~Mpc, we find a combined pulsar timing array echo signal-to-noise ratio of 33, with up to 24 pulsars individually resolving the signal among pulsars with 50-year baselines. The angular dependence of the single-pulsar echo sensitivity alone enables independent sky localization of the source to $\sim$10--100~deg$^2$, and the resolved pulsar-term frequencies directly measure the binary inspiral rate hundreds to thousands of years ago. With sufficient pulsar distance precision, a small set of anchor pulsars could additionally phase-connect the array and trace the post-Newtonian evolution coherently over kpc baselines. The source population required for gravity echoes is drawn from the same massive-end census responsible for the observed nanoHertz stochastic background.

AI.tldr: Combining μHz Earth-term and nHz pulsar-term gravitational wave detections in PTAs allows detailed temporal and spatial study of supermassive black hole binary evolution, potentially enabling sky localization and historical inspiral rate measurements.
AI.motivation: To exploit the information latent in pulsar timing array pulsar terms as gravity echoes of supermassive black hole binary inspirals by combining future μHz-band gravitational wave detections, thereby enhancing the temporal and spatial resolution of binary evolution studies beyond the capabilities of current detectors alone.
AI.method: The method involves analyzing the gravitational wave signals detected by a μHz-band mission and pulsar timing arrays simultaneously, using the Earth term at μHz frequencies and pulsar terms at nHz frequencies to create a temporal baseline and leverage multiple pulsars as separate, dated snapshots of the binary inspiral stage, supported by signal-to-noise ratio calculations and angular sensitivity analysis for sky localization.
AI.result: The paper discusses how future detections of gravitational waves in the microhertz band (μHz), specifically from nearby supermassive black hole binaries, can enable pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) to probe binary evolution via pulsar terms, which act like gravitational wave echoes from earlier inspiral stages. This dual measurement, combining μHz Earth-term signals and nanohertz (nHz) pulsar-term echoes, offers a unique temporal baseline. For a representative binary of 10^9 solar masses at 80 Mpc, a strong combined signal with high signal-to-noise ratio is predicted, and sky localization to tens of square degrees is achievable. High precision in pulsar distances could allow phase-connected analysis across kiloparsec scales, tracing post-Newtonian inspiral dynamics. The source population overlaps with the massive binaries contributing to the nHz stochastic gravitational wave background.
AI.conclusion: Future μHz-band gravitational wave detectors can transform pulsar terms into powerful probes of supermassive black hole binary evolution by providing gravity echoes, enabling source localization, inspiral rate measurement at earlier epochs, and coherent post-Newtonian evolution tracking across pulsar distances.

title: Aspects of gravitational clustering and structure formation in the Universe
summary: The distribution of galaxies, halo abundance, and peculiar velocities are influenced by non-linear gravitational interactions, making the study of non-linear evolution crucial for accurate cosmological predictions. We explore these aspects using N-body simulations. Theoretical models of the halo mass function (HMF) can be formulated without referencing a cosmological model or input power spectrum. HMF obtained from N-body simulations show systematic deviations of 5-20\% from theoretical predictions. The physical origin of deviations may result from cosmology, the power spectrum, or both. We examine HMF deviations from universality for scale-free power spectra with an Einstein-de Sitter cosmology. We demonstrate that the mass function exhibits an explicit dependence on the slope of the input power spectrum. We find that an effective index of the $Λ$CDM model can correspond to the HMF from scale-free cosmologies as a first approximation. Furthermore, structure formation has led to deviations from homogeneity and isotropy on scales up to at least $100$ Mpc/h, expected to affect measurements of $H_0$. We revisit this issue of the concordance model. We find a correlation between errors in $H_0$ estimates and the density around the observer. Further, our mock observations reveal that deviations of up to 5\% can occur in Milky Way-sized halos. While this finding alone does not fully resolve the Hubble tension, it may account for part of it. It is essential to understand the limitations of N-body simulations to avoid misinterpreting data. We show that the missing power at small scales introduces errors in the root-mean-square fluctuations and in the simulated mass function. Our analytical calculation indicates that mode coupling between small and large scales depends on resolving collapsed halos. Therefore, accurate mode coupling estimates require sufficient halos in the simulation.

AI.tldr: This paper uses N-body simulations to explore how non-linear gravitational effects cause deviations in halo mass function predictions and biases in local $H_0$ measurements, highlighting the role of power spectrum slope, local density, and resolution limitations in simulations.
AI.motivation: To address deviations in halo mass function predictions and understand their origin, and to investigate the influence of non-linear gravitational interactions on cosmological observables including the Hubble constant $H_0$.
AI.method: N-body simulations and analytical calculations.
AI.result: N-body simulations reveal 5-20% deviations in HMF from theoretical models; mass function explicitly depends on the slope of the input power spectrum; deviations from homogeneity and isotropy up to at least 100 Mpc/h affect $H_0$ measurements; correlation found between $H_0$ estimation errors and local density; missing small-scale power in simulations causes errors in fluctuations and mass function; mode coupling estimates require sufficient halo resolution.
AI.conclusion: Accurate cosmological predictions require accounting for power spectrum dependencies in HMF, local density effects on $H_0$ measurements, and sufficient resolution in simulations to properly capture mode coupling; these factors partially explain observed discrepancies like the Hubble tension but do not fully resolve them.

title: Archival Multiband Gravitational-Wave Signals from Massive Black Hole Binary Mergers
summary: While massive black hole binaries (MBHBs) merge at gravitational-wave frequencies above the pulsar timing array (PTA) sensitivity band, we show that they leave orphaned low-frequency contributions in the PTA pulsar term. Due to the light-propagation time between each pulsar in the array and Earth, the pulsar term acts as a time-delayed probe of a chirping merger with a specific frequency response determined by the direction of origin and intrinsic properties of the MBHB. We provide a detailed consideration of how such a multiband signal would manifest in a full PTA, demonstrate an approach to stack these orphaned pulsar terms across the array, and discuss prospects for an archival, multiband search in conjunction with MBHB mergers observed in astrometric data or spaceborne interferometers like LISA.

AI.tldr: Massive black hole binary mergers produce delayed low-frequency signals in pulsar timing arrays, which can be stacked and jointly analyzed with data from other observatories to enable multiband gravitational wave detection beyond PTA sensitivity limits.
AI.motivation: To investigate the presence and detectability of low-frequency gravitational wave signals left as orphaned pulsar terms by massive black hole binary mergers beyond the sensitivity band of pulsar timing arrays (PTAs).
AI.method: The paper analyzes the low-frequency pulsar term caused by the light-propagation delay between pulsars and Earth, models the frequency response based on chirping mergers' direction and intrinsic properties, proposes a stacking method to combine pulsar terms across the PTA, and considers joint searches with data from astrometry or space-based interferometers like LISA.
AI.result: The study shows that MBHB mergers produce orphaned low-frequency signals detectable in the pulsar term of PTAs, that these can be coherently combined across the array to enhance detectability, and outlines how these signals could form a multiband gravitational wave signature accessible via archival PTA data and multimessenger collaborations.
AI.conclusion: Orphaned pulsar terms from MBHB mergers provide a new, complementary low-frequency gravitational wave signal for PTAs, enabling multiband detection strategies when combined with other observatories, enhancing future prospects for gravitational wave astronomy.

title: Impact of Primordial Black Hole population on 21 cm observables at high redshift
summary: The 21-cm signal, one of the most promising probes of the high-redshift Universe, has traditionally been modelled without accounting for the effects of active galactic nuclei (AGN) in the pre-JWST era, primarily due to the lack of observational evidence for AGNs at z > 6. However, following the discovery of several AGNs at redshifts as high as z ~ 10 by JWST, it has become imperative to incorporate the impact of these early AGNs when predicting the 21-cm signal. Supposing that these AGNs are seeded by primordial black holes (PBHs), we study their impact with a semi-numerical model setup. Specifically, we extended the explicitly photon-conserving reionization framework, SCRIPT, including essential cosmic dawn physics and PBH contributions. This enables us to compute both the global signal and the power spectrum of the 21-cm line over the redshift range z ~ 30 - 5 within a self-consistent framework. Building on this setup, we then investigate the impact of different PBH mass functions (obeying current observational constraints) on the resulting signal. The X-ray heating from PBHs can substantially make the depth of the global 21-cm signal shallower and suppress the expected power amplitude during cosmic dawn. We also find that the choice of mass function plays a crucial role in shaping the 21-cm signal, and can, in fact, lead to significantly different predictions.

AI.tldr: The paper models the 21-cm signal incorporating early AGNs seeded by primordial black holes, finding that PBHs' X-ray heating modifies the 21-cm signal depth and power spectrum, with mass functions critically influencing the results.
AI.motivation: The recent discovery of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) at very high redshifts (z ~ 10) by JWST necessitates updating models of the 21-cm signal from the early Universe to include AGN impacts, particularly those seeded by primordial black holes (PBHs).
AI.method: An extension of the photon-conserving reionization framework SCRIPT was developed, incorporating cosmic dawn physics and PBH effects, allowing self-consistent computation of the 21-cm global signal and power spectrum from z ~ 30 to 5. Various PBH mass functions consistent with observational constraints were tested for their impact.
AI.result: Including X-ray heating from PBHs significantly alters the predicted 21-cm global signal depth and power spectrum amplitude during cosmic dawn. Different PBH mass functions produce notably varying 21-cm signal predictions.
AI.conclusion: The presence and properties of PBHs, especially their mass functions, must be accounted for in 21-cm signal predictions, as they have a major impact on the signal characteristics during cosmic dawn.

title: An Analytic Threshold for LESA-Driven Negative ELN Flux Directions in Core-Collapse Supernovae: Derivation and Population Census
summary: In core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe), deleptonization normally favors $ν_e$ over $\barν_e$ emission. However, lepton-number emission self-sustained asymmetry (LESA) can make the energy-integrated emitted lepton-number flux negative along some directions. We derive a simple diagnostic for this transition and test it in 33 independent 3D CCSN simulations: 25 Princeton/Fornax models ($8.1$--$100\,M_\odot$) and 8 Garching models, including non-, slow-, and fast-rotating $15\,M_\odot$ cases. Of 23 non-black-hole-forming Princeton models, 22 cross the threshold, with median onset $t_c=225\,\mathrm{ms}$, IQR $162$--$264\,\mathrm{ms}$, and cross-model scatter $\mathrm{CV}=18.6\%$. Full-sky flux-sign searches show that the threshold identifies the anti-LESA-pole transition, distinguishing the global LESA-driven crossing from early localized turbulent crossings. The fast-rotating Garching $15\,M_\odot$ model, where rapid rotation suppresses the LESA dipole, is correctly classified as a non-crosser without using any rotation parameter. Both black-hole-forming Princeton models cross near $250\,\mathrm{ms}$ post-bounce and remain above threshold for $1807$ and $2463\,\mathrm{ms}$ before collapse. Thus, in the next nearby CCSN, the emitted $\barν_e$ energy flux may exceed the $ν_e$ flux along some lines of sight. Such directions may also correlate with sustained fast flavor instability, although testing this requires local phase-space distributions or dedicated linear stability analysis. The relevant quantity here is the energy-integrated emitted flux field, i.e. a luminosity difference per steradian, not a neutrino number flux.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the transition in lepton-number flux asymmetry during core-collapse supernovae, focusing on the occurrence of negative lepton-number flux along certain directions caused by LESA.
AI.motivation: To better understand the directional asymmetries in neutrino emission during core-collapse supernovae caused by LESA and their implications for neutrino flavor evolution and observational signatures.
AI.method: The study derives a simple diagnostic criterion for detecting the sign change in energy-integrated lepton-number flux and applies it to 33 independent 3D CCSN simulations from two groups with varying progenitor masses and rotation rates.
AI.result: Most non-black-hole-forming models cross the threshold for negative lepton-number flux with consistent timing and scatter; fast rotation suppresses LESA-induced transitions; black-hole-forming models also show the transition before collapse; directional negative fluxes may link to fast flavor instabilities.
AI.conclusion: The devised diagnostic effectively identifies the transition in lepton-number flux sign across diverse 3D CCSN simulations, distinguishing between global LESA-driven flux changes and localized turbulence. The results suggest potential observational consequences for neutrino flux in future nearby CCSN events, including correlations with flavor instabilities.

title: Saturation Mechanisms in the Interacting Dark Sector
summary: We introduce a family of phenomenological cosmological models featuring an interacting dark sector modulated by a sparseness scale parameter, in order to describe the late-time accelerated expansion of the universe. The sparseness scale, inspired by well-established saturation mechanisms in ecology and biology, is introduced in the interaction as a half-saturation constant that bounds the energy exchange between dark matter and dark energy, controls the dynamical behaviour of the physical variables and can prevent the phantom crossing. We consider three nonlinear interacting models, where two of them recover the linear interacting scenarios when the sparsity parameter vanishes. We examine the phase-space of the cosmological field equations by using the Hubble normalization approach. We determine the stationary points and their stability properties in order to reconstruct the asymptotics behaviour of the field equations. Such an analysis allows us to demonstrate the effects of the sparseness scale on the background dynamics. We test the interacting models with observational data. Specifically, we employ Supernovae catalogues, cosmic chronometers, Baryon Acoustic Oscillation measurements from DESI DR2, and redshift-space distortion measurements of the growth of large-scale structure through the $f$ and $fσ_8$ observables. The Bayesian analysis suggests that, for two of the three models, a vanishing sparsity parameter is disfavoured at more than the 95\% confidence interval, providing observational support for a nonzero sparseness scale in the dark sector interaction.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes nonlinear interacting dark sector cosmological models featuring a sparseness scale to explain late-time accelerated expansion, demonstrates their dynamical behavior via phase-space analysis, and supports the models observationally, showing evidence for a nonzero sparseness parameter controlling dark matter-dark energy interaction.
AI.motivation: To introduce and analyze phenomenological cosmological models with an interacting dark sector modulated by a sparseness scale parameter, aiming to explain the late-time accelerated expansion of the universe and to prevent phantom crossing in dark matter-dark energy interactions.
AI.method: The paper introduces three nonlinear interacting cosmological models featuring a sparseness scale as a half-saturation constant. It studies the phase-space of the cosmological field equations using the Hubble normalization approach, determines stationary points and their stability, and reconstructs asymptotic behavior. The models are then tested against observational data including Supernovae, cosmic chronometers, Baryon Acoustic Oscillations from DESI DR2, and redshift-space distortion measurements of large-scale structure growth through f and fσ_8 observables using Bayesian analysis.
AI.result: The analysis shows that the sparseness scale modulates the background dynamics and bounds the energy exchange between dark matter and dark energy. Observational data disfavor a zero sparsity parameter at more than 95% confidence for two of the three models, supporting the existence of a nonzero sparseness scale in dark sector interactions.
AI.conclusion: The introduction of a sparseness scale parameter in the dark sector interaction provides a viable mechanism to describe late-time accelerated expansion, controlling dynamical behavior and avoiding phantom crossing. Observational evidence supports a nonzero sparseness scale, indicating the importance of nonlinear effects in dark matter-dark energy interactions.

title: Geometry, Not Calorimetry, Drives the Radio/Infrared/Gamma-Ray Correlation
summary: We investigate whether the observed radio-infrared-$γ$-ray correlation in star-forming galaxies is a geometric effect rather than a signature of local cosmic-ray (CR) calorimetry. Using the GALPROP framework, we generate synthetic observations for external viewers from a grid of 3D Milky Way models with varied CR source, gas, interstellar radiation, and magnetic field distributions, all normalised to reproduce local CR data. We find that a tight, quasi-linear correlation arises naturally from line-of-sight integration through the extended, radially-structured disc, even when local calorimetry is absent. The correlation's properties depend strongly on viewing geometry, preserving its form under moderate inclination but breaking down in edge-on views where galactic components are stratified. We conclude that the correlation is primarily an emergent property of geometric projection, not local physics. This implies that its scatter is likely not random noise but a diagnostic of underlying galactic structure and viewing angle.

AI.tldr: The radio-infrared-γ-ray correlation in star-forming galaxies arises mainly from geometric projection effects rather than local cosmic-ray calorimetry, with observational scatter reflecting galactic structure and viewing angle.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the observed multiwavelength emission correlation in star-forming galaxies is intrinsically related to cosmic-ray physics (local calorimetry) or primarily a geometric projection effect, thereby clarifying the physical interpretation of these correlations.
AI.method: Utilized the GALPROP framework to simulate synthetic observations based on 3D Milky Way models that vary cosmic-ray sources, gas, interstellar radiation, and magnetic field distributions, all normalized to local cosmic-ray measurements. The analysis involved examining line-of-sight integrations in different viewing geometries to assess correlation properties.
AI.result: The paper investigates the nature of the observed correlation between radio, infrared, and γ-ray emissions in star-forming galaxies. By employing the GALPROP framework, the authors create synthetic observations from 3D Milky Way models with varied cosmic-ray source distributions and galactic components, normalized to local cosmic-ray data. They discover that the quasi-linear correlation is largely a geometric effect caused by line-of-sight integration through the galaxy's radially-structured disc, rather than a direct consequence of local cosmic-ray calorimetry processes. The correlation varies significantly with viewing geometry, maintaining form under moderate inclinations but breaking down in edge-on perspectives. This suggests the correlation's scatter encodes structural and geometric information about galaxies rather than random noise.
AI.conclusion: The tight radio-infrared-γ-ray correlation is primarily an emergent product of geometric projection through galaxy discs, not local cosmic-ray calorimetry. Its scatter serves as a diagnostic for galactic structure and viewing geometry.

title: Bayesian Inference of Dense-Matter Equations of State from Small-Radius Compact Stars with Twin-Star Scenarios
summary: We investigate dense-matter equations of state (EOSs) within a Bayesian framework, with particular emphasis on whether recent small-radius compact-star candidates can be accommodated in a twin-star scenario. For the hadronic sector, we adopt a meta-modeling EOS constrained by the NICER mass--radius measurements of PSR J0030$+$0451, PSR J0437$-$4715, PSR J0614$-$3329, and the massive pulsar PSR J0740$+$6620. The hadronic inference indicates that PSR J0614$-$3329 favors a somewhat softer EOS than the other two \(\sim1.4\,M_\odot\) pulsars, while the \(\sim2\,M_\odot\) constraint prevents the EOS from becoming too soft. We then introduce a strong first-order phase transition through a constant-speed-of-sound quark-matter segment. Using HESS J1731$-$347 and XTE J1814$-$338 to constrain the phase-transition parameters, we find a preferred transition density of \(n_\mathrm{t}\sim2.7\text{--}2.8\,n_0\), a sizable energy-density jump of \(600\text{--}700\) MeV, and a relatively large post-transition sound speed of \(c_s^2/c^2\sim0.85\). Such a phase transition generates a disconnected hybrid branch with radii of about \(6\text{--}7\) km at masses around \(1.2\text{--}1.4\,M_\odot\), and strongly suppresses the dimensionless tidal deformability relative to the purely hadronic branch. This pronounced change in tidal deformability is a characteristic signature of the twin-star mechanism and may provide an important observational tool for identifying phase transitions in neutron-star matter in future multimessenger measurements. These results show that small-radius compact stars can provide direct constraints on both the strength of a first-order phase transition and the stiffness of the post-transition phase in dense matter.

AI.tldr: This paper uses Bayesian modeling of dense matter EOSs combined with astronomical data to show that a strong first-order phase transition can explain small-radius compact stars as twin stars and predict observable signals, like reduced tidal deformability, useful for future neutron-star studies.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether recent observations of compact stars with small radii can be explained within a twin-star scenario involving a first-order phase transition in dense matter equations of state (EOS).
AI.method: Adopt a meta-modeling EOS for hadronic matter constrained by NICER mass-radius measurements of several pulsars; introduce a strong first-order phase transition modeled by a constant-speed-of-sound quark matter segment; constrain phase transition parameters using observational data from specific compact-star candidates (HESS J1731-347 and XTE J1814-338).
AI.result: Identification of preferred phase-transition parameters: transition density around 2.7-2.8 times nuclear saturation density, large energy-density jump (600-700 MeV), and high post-transition sound speed (around 0.85 c^2). The phase transition produces a disconnected hybrid branch with small radii (6-7 km) at masses 1.2-1.4 solar masses and significantly reduces tidal deformability compared to purely hadronic stars.
AI.conclusion: Small-radius compact stars can directly constrain key properties of a strong first-order phase transition in dense matter, including transition strength and stiffness of the post-transition phase. The marked change in tidal deformability serves as a potential observational signature of the twin-star mechanism, aiding future identification of phase transitions in neutron-star matter via multimessenger observations.

title: Energy Loss of Newborn Magnetars by Schwinger Process
summary: We investigate electron--positron pair creation through the Schwinger process in newborn magnetars with millisecond spin periods and surface dipole fields close to or above the QED critical field, $B_{\rm Q} = 4.414\times10^{13}\,\mathrm{G}$. In the unscreened field scenario, we derive the analytical global pair creation flux and recast it into a compact form with accurate analytic approximations. For a fiducial model with $B_{\rm p} = 10^{14}\,\mathrm{G}$ and $P_0 = 1\,\mathrm{ms}$, the Schwinger channel exceeds the classical Goldreich--Julian particle supply by many orders of magnitude and becomes the dominant source of charges at the earliest stage of the magnetar. The associated discharge removes about $90\%$ of the initial rotational energy within 30 ms, suppresses the gravitational-wave loss channel, and implies that the observable millisecond phase is extremely short in this unscreened scenario. The rapid energy release over such a short timescale may also provide a viable power source for astrophysical transients. Extending the same fiducial model to $10^4\,\mathrm{yr}$ gives spin periods of order seconds, linking newborn millisecond magnetars to the mature magnetar population.

AI.tldr: In newborn magnetars with extremely strong magnetic fields and millisecond periods, electron-positron pair creation via the Schwinger process dominates particle supply, rapidly dissipating rotational energy and linking early millisecond phases to longer-period mature magnetars.
AI.motivation: To investigate the electron-positron pair creation process through the Schwinger mechanism in newborn magnetars with very strong magnetic fields and rapid rotation, and its implications for the magnetar's evolution and observable phenomena.
AI.method: The paper derives analytical expressions for pair creation flux in highly magnetized newborn magnetars, uses approximations to simplify results, and applies the model to estimate energy loss and spin evolution over milliseconds to thousands of years.
AI.result: The Schwinger pair creation rate significantly exceeds the classical Goldreich-Julian particle supply, dominating charge production at the earliest magnetar stages. This discharge rapidly removes about 90% of the initial rotational energy within 30 ms, suppresses gravitational-wave losses, and predicts a very brief observable millisecond phase. Over 10^4 years, the spin period evolves to seconds, connecting newborn millisecond magnetars to mature magnetars.
AI.conclusion: The Schwinger pair creation mechanism in newborn magnetars profoundly impacts their early rotational energy loss, shortening the observable millisecond phase and providing a potential energy source for transient astrophysical phenomena; it also explains the spin evolution toward mature magnetar periods.

title: Multi-wavelength study of EP250416a / GRB 250416C: An Optically Dark Long GRB with a Late Jet Break
comment: 12 pages, 14 figures, 4 tables, submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: We present multi-wavelength study of the $γ$/X-ray transient EP250416a (also designated GRB 250416C), triggered by the Einstein Probe (EP) Wide-field X-ray Telescope and also by SVOM and Konus-Wind. Observations spanning the gamma-ray, X-ray, and optical bands facilitated detailed analysis of the burst's prompt emission, afterglow evolution, and physical origin. EP250416a exhibits a burst duration of 30 s in X-ray and 17.7 s in gamma-rays, with joint spectral fitting of 0.5-5000 keV data gives $E\rm_{peak}=342_{-232}^{+90}$ keV. Optical spectroscopy of the afterglow, acquired with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) on Gemini South, yielded a redshift of $z=0.963$. Accounting for the measured redshift, the isotropic energies are $E\rm_{X,iso}=2.7_{-0.5}^{+0.9}\times10^{50}$ erg and $E\rm_{γ,iso}=7.34_{-2.1}^{+5.1}\times10^{51}$ erg, aligning with the Amati relation for long GRBs. The fluence ratio $\rm S(25-50~keV)/S(50-100~keV)=0.78_{-0.15}^{+0.1}$ classifies EP250416a as an X-ray rich (XRR) GRB. The X-ray afterglow shows an initial shallow decay ($α\approx -0.5$) transitioning to a canonical decay phase ($α\approx -1$), with a very late jet break at $t\sim 1.5\times 10^6$ s, corresponding to a jet half-opening angle of $θ_j=10.6_{-1.8}^{+1.9}$ degrees. EP250416a is optically dark, as it shows only a faint $r$-band detection ($r=24.16$ mag) from Gemini South-GMOS and a low optical-to-X-ray spectral index $β_{\rm OX} = 0.3$. This may be attributed to significant host-galaxy extinction, with a required $A_V^{\text{host}}=5.5\ \text{mag}$ derived from the extinction curve model.

AI.tldr: Multi-wavelength observations of GRB 250416C reveal a long, X-ray rich burst with typical energetics and jet angles for long GRBs, but with a heavily obscured, optically faint afterglow due to host dust extinction.
AI.motivation: To conduct a detailed multi-wavelength analysis of the gamma-ray/X-ray transient EP250416a (GRB 250416C) to characterize its emission properties, physical origin, and afterglow behavior.
AI.method: We employed multi-instrument triggers to gather prompt and afterglow data across gamma-ray, X-ray, and optical bands; performed spectral fitting and redshift measurement via spectroscopy; analyzed afterglow decay light curves; and modeled extinction to explain optical faintness.
AI.result: EP250416a has a burst duration of 30 s (X-ray) and 17.7 s (gamma-ray), with peak energy at 342 keV, redshift z=0.963; isotropic energies consistent with long GRB Amati relation; classified as X-ray rich GRB; X-ray afterglow showing canonical decay and late jet break with opening angle ~10.6 degrees; optically dark afterglow implying significant host extinction (A_V ~5.5 mag).
AI.conclusion: EP250416a is a typical long-duration X-ray rich GRB with an optically dark afterglow likely caused by substantial host-galaxy extinction. Its measured properties support the standard burst origin and afterglow model including jet collimation effects.

title: Gauging the Impact of Cosmic Ray Feedback on the Stellar Initial Mass Function
comment: 17 Pages, 9 Figures, published in ApJ. arXiv admin note: text overlap with arXiv:2407.17597
summary: Cosmic rays (CRs) drive ionization and influence gas dynamics in molecular clouds (MCs), potentially impacting the resulting star formation outcomes. Although previous simulations of individual star formation have included methods for cosmic ray transport (CRT), none have been large enough to resolve the stellar initial mass function (IMF). We conduct numerical simulations following the collapse of a $20000 M_{\odot}$ MC and the subsequent star formation including CRT, both with and without CRs accelerated by winds from the young massive stars, and compare against a non-CRT simulation. We show that after the first massive stars form, the cavity produced by feedback is more pronounced in the CRT simulations because the external CRs are able to propagate inwards and compress the gas into higher density structures. This increases the subsequent star formation in the cloud; by the end of the simulation, the SFE in the CRT simulation including stellar wind CRs is 43 \% higher than the non-CRT simulation. The IMF is also top heavy in comparison, with a slope above 1 $M_{\odot}$ that is shallower by $\sim 20$ \%. These effects are also present in the simulation without wind-accelerated CRs, but they are not as pronounced; the SFE is only 16 \% higher than the non-CRT simulation, and the IMF high-mass slope is shallower by $\sim 10$ \%. These results may explain some of the observed top-heavy IMFs, which typically occur in high-CR environments such as the galactic center.

AI.tldr: This study uses large-scale simulations of molecular cloud collapse including cosmic ray transport to show that cosmic rays, particularly those from massive star winds, increase star formation efficiency and produce a top-heavy stellar initial mass function, helping to explain observations in high cosmic ray environments.
AI.motivation: To investigate the impact of cosmic ray transport (CRT) on star formation and the stellar initial mass function (IMF) within large molecular clouds, addressing the gap that previous CRT simulations did not resolve the IMF at large scales.
AI.method: Numerical simulations of a 20000 solar mass molecular cloud collapse and subsequent star formation were conducted, incorporating cosmic ray transport both with and without cosmic rays accelerated by young massive star winds, compared against a simulation without CRT.
AI.result: Simulations with CRT showed more pronounced feedback cavities and inward propagation of cosmic rays compressing gas into denser structures, leading to increased star formation efficiency (SFE) and a top-heavy IMF. Specifically, SFE increased by 43% with stellar wind CRs and IMF slope above 1 solar mass was ~20% shallower compared to non-CRT. Without wind-accelerated CRs, SFE increased by 16% and IMF slope was ~10% shallower. These findings may explain observed top-heavy IMFs in high cosmic ray environments.
AI.conclusion: Cosmic ray transport, especially including cosmic rays from stellar winds, significantly influences star formation outcomes by enhancing gas compression, increasing star formation efficiency, and producing a top-heavy initial mass function, paralleling observations in high-CR regions like galactic centers.

title: Magnetar Engines in Broad-lined Type Ic Supernovae and a Unified Picture for Magnetar-powered Stripped-envelope Supernovae
comment: 39 pages, 17 figures, 3 tables, Comments are welcome!
summary: We model the multi-band lightcurves of 80 SNe Ic-BL, including 11 associated with lGRBs, using a magnetar engine model with $^{56}$Ni decay. We find that the data are all consistent with a magnetar central engine, and such a model yields high-quality fits across the sample. The medians with $1σ$ regions of the key parameters are $P_{\rm{i}}\sim2.04^{+1.84}_{-0.96}\,{\rm{ms}}$, $B_{\rm{p}}\sim3.96^{+3.28}_{-1.40}\times10^{15}\,{\rm{G}}$, $M_{\rm{ej}}\sim2.30^{+1.48}_{-1.02}\,M_\odot$, and $M_{\rm{Ni}}\sim0.18^{+0.14}_{-0.09}\,M_\odot$, with strong and statistically significant correlations observed for both $M_{\rm{ej}}-P_{\rm{i}}$ (anti-correlation) and $M_{\rm{Ni}}-M_{\rm{ej}}$ (correlation). Comparing the SN Ic-BL samples with and without lGRB association using fitting parameters, we find no significant difference between them, although the GRB-associated sample is slightly brighter, possibly due to an observational bias. Relative to ordinary SNe Ic, SNe Ic-BL have similar $^{56}$Ni and ejecta masses, suggesting comparable pre-SN progenitor properties, with differences possibly arising from the presence of a magnetar engine. In comparison with other possible magnetar-powered SESNe, including SLSNe Ic and FBOTs, we confirm a strong universal $M_{\rm{ej}}-P_{\rm{i}}$ correlation, indicating a common origin. SNe Ic-BL and SLSNe Ic have similar ejecta mass distributions, typically $M_{\rm ej}\gtrsim0.5\,M_\odot$, while FBOTs mostly lie below this value. Differences between SNe Ic-BL and SLSNe Ic may arise from magnetar properties, with SN Ic-BL magnetars rotating faster and having stronger fields. Moreover, the $P_{\rm{i}}-B_{\rm{p}}$ distribution of lGRB magnetars largely overlaps with that of SN Ic-BL magnetars. In connection with binary simulation results, we propose a unified physical classification and progenitor framework for magnetar-powered and ordinary SESNe.

AI.tldr: This study models 80 SNe Ic-BL lightcurves with a magnetar engine plus 56Ni decay, finding consistent fits and correlations in their physical parameters. No major differences exist between those with or without lGRBs. Comparison with other supernova types supports a universal magnetar-powered origin and leads to a unified classification framework.
AI.motivation: To understand the central engine mechanism powering SNe Ic-BL including those associated with lGRBs, and to compare their physical properties with other magnetar-powered supernovae and ordinary SNe Ic.
AI.method: Modeling multi-band lightcurves of 80 SNe Ic-BL using a magnetar engine model combined with 56Ni decay, fitting key parameters such as initial spin period, magnetic field, ejecta mass, and nickel mass, and conducting statistical correlation and comparative analysis between samples.
AI.result: The magnetar engine model fits all lightcurve data well, with median parameters identified and significant correlations found between ejecta mass and initial spin period (anti-correlation), and between nickel mass and ejecta mass (correlation). No major differences were found in the parameters between lGRB-associated and non-associated SNe Ic-BL, though the former tend to be slightly brighter. Comparison with ordinary SNe Ic suggests similar progenitors, differing mainly by the presence of a magnetar engine. There is a confirmed universal correlation among magnetar-powered SESNe, and magnetar properties differ between SNe Ic-BL and SLSNe Ic. The distribution of magnetar parameters for lGRB-associated SNe overlaps largely with those of SNe Ic-BL. A unified progenitor framework encompassing magnetar-powered and ordinary SESNe is proposed.
AI.conclusion: The magnetar central engine model effectively explains the observed properties of SNe Ic-BL, including those linked with lGRBs, supporting a continuum of magnetar-powered supernovae with shared physical origins and emphasizing the role of magnetar properties in differentiating supernova types. A unified classification and progenitor model integrating magnetar-powered and ordinary SESNe enhances understanding of their nature and origins.

title: An RXTE Search for the Sterile Neutrino Decay in Galaxy Clusters
summary: We have searched for the 3.55 keV line from sterile neutrino decay using 3.1 megaseconds of RXTE cluster data. A 2.5$σ$ excess of emission over a thermal model is found over the energy span of the 3.55 keV line in the combined spectra of the eight clusters that individually have an excess. The residuals are added to increase the signal to noise ratio of the excess, which is then modeled with a Gaussian to simulate the instrumental spectral response. We find a significant correlation (r = 0.76) for a line centered at 3.6 keV with a model flux of 3.07 x 10$^{-5}$ ph cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. Mixing angle for detected clusters ranges from 0.35 to 6.2 x 10$^{-10}$. The decay rate inferred from the line flux is strongly correlated (r = 0.87) with cluster temperature, which is due to hotter, more massive clusters having a larger amount of dark matter. Approximately half of the decay line total flux comes from the Coma cluster. We fit the Coma cluster spectrum with two different three-component models. The first includes a Gaussian fixed at 3.55 keV to model soft emission. The second three-component model uses a second thermal component to model soft emission. The model fit parameters indicate that the second thermal component is modeling high-energy residuals rather than low ones, where the Gaussian is. Though our line fluxes exceed most reported detections and upper limits, they do not overproduce the dark matter. We conclude that some fraction of the marginally detected excess could be attributed to the decay line since low-temperature thermal emission and systematics fail to model it completely.

AI.tldr: Analysis of RXTE cluster data reveals a 2.5 sigma excess near 3.55 keV potentially from sterile neutrino decay, correlating with cluster temperature and consistent with dark matter constraints, suggesting a partial dark matter decay origin for the emission line.
AI.motivation: The study aims to investigate the presence of a 3.55 keV emission line that could be indicative of sterile neutrino decay, a potential dark matter signature, in galaxy cluster data.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 3.1 megaseconds of RXTE cluster X-ray data, combining spectra from eight clusters showing individual excesses to increase signal-to-noise ratio. They modeled the excess emission using Gaussian components to simulate instrumental response and compared multi-component fits for the Coma cluster dataset.
AI.result: A 2.5 sigma excess emission near 3.55 keV was found, with a significant correlation (r=0.76) for a line centered at 3.6 keV and a flux of 3.07 x 10⁻⁵ ph cm⁻² s⁻¹. The inferred mixing angles range from 0.35 to 6.2 x 10⁻¹⁰, and the decay rate correlates strongly with cluster temperature (r=0.87). The Coma cluster contributes about half of the total flux, and model fits suggest residual emission not fully accounted for by thermal components. The observed line fluxes exceed many previous limits but remain consistent with dark matter constraints.
AI.conclusion: The detected marginal excess emission around 3.55 keV likely includes a contribution from sterile neutrino decay, as standard thermal emission models and systematics cannot fully explain it. This supports a dark matter decay origin for at least part of the signal.

title: Mitigating Systematic Errors in Parameter Estimation of Binary Black Hole Mergers in O1-O3 LIGO-Virgo Data
comment: 23 pages, 13 figures, 2 tables. Comments are welcome
summary: Systematic errors in the parameter estimation (PE) of gravitational wave (GW) mergers can arise from various sources, including waveform systematics, noise mischaracterization, data analysis artifacts, and other unknown factors. In this study, we analyze selected events from the first three observing runs of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) collaboration. We choose events that have been flagged in various studies as potentially affected by systematic errors. Here, we reanalyze these events using a couple of parametric models developed in previous work that incorporate uncertainties in both the phase and amplitude of the GW waveform. In this data-driven approach, we apply sufficiently broad priors on the uncertainty parameters to account for potential systematic errors. Our findings show that the proposed method effectively reduces systematic errors, even those arising from data artifacts, such as glitches occurring near a signal and the deglitching process in GW frame files. Similarly, inconsistent results from different waveform models become much more consistent in our framework. One noteworthy event we examine is GW191109\_010717, which is particularly interesting due to its anti-aligned spin properties. We report that, within our framework, the event still exhibits anti-aligned spin characteristics, but the inference results become consistent across raw and deglitched frame files, as well as across the waveform models used for this event (IMRPhenomXPHM, IMRPhenomXO4a, and NRSur7dq4). A similar trend is observed for the event GW200129\_065458, which previously yielded a high, but inconsistent precession parameter among different waveform models. In contrast, we observe a non-zero and consistent value of $χ_{p}=0.60^{+0.31}_{-0.33}, 0.58^{+0.30}_{-0.29}$ and $0.56^{+0.31}_{-0.28}$ for the IMRPhenomXPHM, IMRPhenomXO4a, and NRSur7dq4 waveform models, respectively.

AI.tldr: This study reanalyzes selected gravitational wave events flagged for systematic errors using parametric models that incorporate waveform uncertainties, significantly improving consistency across waveform models and data conditions.
AI.motivation: Systematic errors in gravitational wave parameter estimation can arise from waveform modeling inaccuracies, noise mischaracterization, and data analysis artifacts, leading to inconsistencies in inferred source properties; this study aims to address these issues using an uncertainty-informed modeling framework.
AI.method: A data-driven approach is applied using parametric models that incorporate uncertainties in gravitational waveform phase and amplitude with broad priors to account for systematic errors, analyzing flagged LVK events across multiple waveform models and data conditions including raw and deglitched data.
AI.result: The method reduces systematic errors including those from data glitches, yielding more consistent parameter estimates across waveform models and data types. For example, anti-aligned spin properties and precession parameters become consistent and robust in the reanalyzed events GW191109_010717 and GW200129_065458.
AI.conclusion: The proposed data-driven approach effectively mitigates systematic errors in gravitational wave parameter estimation, yielding consistent inference results across different waveform models and data conditions for challenging events like GW191109_010717 and GW200129_065458.

title: Testing solitonic boson star interpretations of Sagittarius A* with near-infrared flare astrometry
summary: We use GRAVITY near-infrared (NIR) flare astrometry to test whether Sagittarius A* could be a solitonic boson star. We consider five spherically symmetric solitonic boson-star models with different effective radii, together with the Schwarzschild black hole. Treating the flares as hot spots on circular equatorial orbits, we analyze their centroid motions and images in these spacetimes and use them for parameter fitting. We perform the fitting using both $χ^2$ analysis and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, which yield consistent results: the inferred masses of boson-star models are systematically larger than the established value of $4.3\times10^6M_\odot$. Notably, more diffusive boson stars exhibit imaging properties closer to those of a black hole, leading to mass estimates that are correspondingly closer to the established value. Overall, our results place stringent constraints on solitonic boson star interpretations of Sagittarius A*, although do not completely rule them out.

AI.tldr: This study uses near-infrared flare astrometry data to test if Sagittarius A* could be a solitonic boson star, finding that while boson star models generally imply larger masses than observed, more diffusive models approach black hole signatures but overall impose tight constraints on the boson star scenario without fully excluding it.
AI.motivation: To test the hypothesis that Sagittarius A* could be a solitonic boson star by comparing observational flare astrometry data against theoretical models of such boson stars versus a black hole.
AI.method: Using GRAVITY near-infrared flare astrometry, the study models Sagittarius A* flares as hot spots on circular equatorial orbits in five spherically symmetric solitonic boson-star spacetimes and the Schwarzschild black hole, analyzing centroid motions and images for parameter fitting with χ² and Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods.
AI.result: The inferred boson-star masses are consistently larger than the established value of 4.3×10⁶ solar masses, with more diffusive boson star models producing imaging characteristics more similar to black holes and thus yielding mass estimates closer to the established value.
AI.conclusion: The analysis provides stringent constraints on interpreting Sagittarius A* as a solitonic boson star, showing systematic deviations in mass estimates but not completely ruling out these models as possible explanations.
